title: No. 13 — Advantage of the Union in Respect to Economy in Government (Hamilton)
paragraphs: Closely tied to the question of revenue is the question of economy. Money saved in one area can be put to good use in another, and that much less needs to be drawn from the people's pockets. If the States are united under one government, only one national civil service must be supported. If they are split into several confederacies, each will need its own national civil service. Each one, in its principal departments, must be just as large as a government for the whole would be. Splitting the States into thirteen unconnected sovereignties is too extravagant and too dangerous a plan to attract many supporters. Those who speculate about dismembering the empire usually imagine three confederacies: one of the four Northern States, another of the four Middle States, and a third of the five Southern States. It is unlikely there would be more than that. Under this division, each confederacy would cover more territory than the kingdom of Great Britain. No well-informed person would suppose that such a confederacy could be properly governed by something less comprehensive than the plan proposed by the convention. When a State reaches a certain size, it requires the same governmental energy and the same forms of administration as a much larger one. This cannot be demonstrated with precision, since there is no rule by which to measure the civil power needed to govern a given number of people. But the island of Britain is roughly the same size as each of these supposed confederacies and contains about eight million people. Considering the authority required to direct the passions of so large a society toward the public good, we can see no reason to doubt that a similar amount of power would suffice for an even larger society. Civil power, properly organized and used, can extend its force across great distances. It can, in effect, reproduce itself throughout a great empire by the careful arrangement of subordinate institutions.

The idea that each confederacy would require a government no less comprehensive than the one proposed becomes stronger when we consider an even more probable scenario. A division into three confederacies is one alternative to a general Union, but two is more likely. If we look carefully at geography, commerce, and the habits and prejudices of the different States, we conclude that in the case of disunion they would most naturally combine into two governments. The four Eastern States, bound by every tie of national sympathy and connection, would certainly unite. New York, given its location, would never be foolish enough to leave a weak and unsupported flank exposed to that confederacy. Other obvious reasons would also encourage New York to join. New Jersey is too small to consider being a frontier State against this still more powerful combination, and there appear to be no obstacles to its admission. Even Pennsylvania would have strong reasons to join the Northern league. An active foreign commerce based on her own shipping is her true policy, matching the opinions and dispositions of her citizens. The Southern States, for various reasons, may not see themselves as much interested in encouraging shipping. They may prefer a system that allows all nations unlimited freedom to carry and purchase their goods. Pennsylvania may not want to entangle her interests with a connection so contrary to her policy. Since she must in any case be a frontier, she may judge it safer to have her exposed side facing the weaker Southern Confederacy rather than the stronger Northern one. This would give her the best chance of avoiding becoming the Flanders of America. Whatever Pennsylvania decides, if the Northern Confederacy includes New Jersey, there is unlikely to be more than one confederacy to the south.

Nothing could be more obvious than that thirteen States can support a national government better than half or a third or any number short of the whole. This consideration alone undercuts the objection to the proposed plan based on expense. That objection, when examined more closely, turns out at every angle to rest on a mistake.

Beyond the question of multiple civil services, consider the people who would have to be employed to police inland trade between the different confederacies against smuggling—a force that would inevitably arise from the demands of revenue. Add the military establishments that would unavoidably result from rivalries and conflicts between the several nations into which the States would be split. Then it becomes clear that separation would be just as harmful to economy as it would be to peace, commerce, revenue, and liberty in every part.
